quote: Diese Sätze über Bunddiscriminanten sind war- scheinlich garnicht richtig.
english: These theorems about Bund discriminants are probably not correct at all.
topic: The page discusses discriminants of algebraic fields (Körper) and of an algebraic 'Bund', the claimed theorem D(y,x)=D(x,y), a note doubting these theorems, and the start of a generalisation of Picard's theorems.

triage.modern_statement: This can't be pinned down precisely. Going by the page context, Hilbert seems to have defined a discriminant D(y,x) for an algebraic 'Bund'. This was probably a system of algebraic functions in two variables, or a field of algebraic functions in x and y. He then claimed the symmetry D(y,x)=D(x,y), meaning the discriminant is the same whichever variable is treated as independent. One possible modern reading is the discriminant (or different) of a two-variable function field taken over k(x) and over k(y). For the most naive reading, the discriminants of a plane curve f(x,y)=0 with respect to y and with respect to x, the two are not equal in general. Hilbert's note, which says the theorems are probably not correct at all, rejects his own claim. Without his definition of 'Bund' and of D, the exact statement can't be reconstructed.
triage.answered_by: No one, as far as I can find. Hilbert himself wrote on the same page that the claimed theorems were probably false. I found no published follow-up, and the claim is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.
triage.why: My search for Hilbert's 'Bund' discriminants and the claimed identity D(y,x)=D(x,y) turned up nothing relevant: no secondary literature, no edition of the notebook, and no later work. The note is a self-correction on a private sketch whose central term ('Bund') is undefined in what we have. That means it can't be matched to a specific modern theorem or open problem. Under the naive reading for plane curves, the two discriminants differ, which fits Hilbert's own doubt. This reading is my inference and isn't backed by a source. The note is not one of Hilbert's published problems.
